1.summary: After Moses' death God commissions Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan, telling him to be strong and courageous and to keep the law, and the eastern tribes pledge to follow him.
1.lookfor: Count how often Joshua is told to be strong and courageous, notice what success depends on, and listen to the eastern tribes' reply.

names.name: Joshua
names.gloss: Son of Nun of the tribe of Ephraim, Moses' assistant and now his successor.

names.name: Reubenites
names.gloss: The tribe of Reuben, already settled east of the Jordan.

names.name: Gadites
names.gloss: The tribe of Gad, also settled east of the Jordan.

insights.title: After the death of Moses
insights.body: The book opens, "after the death of Moses the servant of Yahweh" (1:1). Moses, the only leader Israel had known, is gone, and God speaks directly to Joshua. The promise does not depend on one great man: "As I was with Moses, so I will be with you" (1:5).

insights.title: Strong and courageous
insights.body: Joshua is told "Be strong and courageous" three times by God (1:6, 1:7, 1:9) and once more by the people (1:18). Moses had already given him the same charge. The repetition suggests Joshua needed it.

insights.title: Meditate day and night
insights.body: "This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night" (1:8). The military leader's first instruction is about Scripture. Psalm 1 uses the same language for the blessed person who meditates on God's law day and night.

insights.title: Hagah: to murmur
insights.body: The Hebrew verb behind "meditate" (1:8), hagah, means to murmur or mutter, the sound of reading half aloud. Meditation in ancient Israel was not silent emptying of the mind but repeating God's words over and over.

insights.title: Every place your foot treads
insights.body: "I have given you every place that the sole of your foot will tread on, as I told Moses" (1:3). The borders reach to the Euphrates (1:4), the widest description of the promise, matching God's word to Abraham.

insights.title: The eastern tribes' promise
insights.body: Joshua reminds Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh of their pledge to fight before their brothers (1:13-15). Their reply goes further: "All that you have commanded us we will do" (1:16), and anyone who rebels will die (1:18). Chapter 22 shows them keeping their word.

insights.title: Wherever you go
insights.body: God promises, "Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go" (1:9). What new territory are you facing where you need that promise?

2.summary: Joshua sends two spies to Jericho, where Rahab hides them, confesses that Yahweh is God, and secures a promise that her family will be spared when she ties a scarlet cord in her window.
2.lookfor: Notice how Rahab outwits the king's men, what she has heard about Israel's God, and the sign she is given.

names.name: Shittim
names.gloss: Israel's last camp east of the Jordan; the name means "acacia trees."

names.name: Jericho
names.gloss: An ancient walled city near the Jordan, one of the oldest towns in the world.

names.name: Rahab
names.gloss: A prostitute in Jericho whose house was built into the city wall.

names.name: Sihon
names.gloss: Amorite king east of the Jordan defeated by Israel.

names.name: Og
names.gloss: King of Bashan, also defeated by Israel.

insights.title: Flax on the roof
insights.body: Rahab hides the spies "under the stalks of flax which she had laid in order on the roof" (2:6). Flat roofs were used for drying flax, which was soaked and dried before being made into linen. The detail fits the season of harvest mentioned in the next chapter.

insights.title: A house in the wall
insights.body: Rahab's house "was on the side of the wall, and she lived on the wall" (2:15). Some ancient cities had houses built into or between double walls. It made her house ideal for an escape and, later, the one part of the wall that mattered most.

insights.title: Rahab's confession
insights.body: "Yahweh your God, he is God in heaven above, and on earth beneath" (2:11). A Canaanite prostitute uses almost the same words Moses used in Deuteronomy. She has heard what God did at the Red Sea and to Sihon and Og (2:10), and draws the right conclusion where Israel's spies once failed.

insights.title: Chesed: kindness
insights.body: Rahab asks the spies to swear that, "since I have dealt kindly with you" they will "deal kindly" with her family (2:12). The word is chesed, covenant loyalty. A Canaanite woman becomes the first person in the land to be shown the faithfulness God shows Israel.

insights.title: The scarlet cord
insights.body: The scarlet line in the window marks the house to be spared (2:18), much as the Passover blood marked Israel's houses in Egypt. Early Christian writers, beginning with Clement of Rome, saw in the scarlet cord a picture of redemption through Christ's blood.

insights.title: Rahab in the New Testament
insights.body: Matthew lists Rahab among Jesus' ancestors as the mother of Boaz. Hebrews praises her faith, and James her works. All three keep the title "Rahab the prostitute," showing that her past did not prevent her welcome.

insights.title: Their hearts melted
insights.body: Rahab says, "our hearts melted" when Jericho heard of Israel (2:11). Forty years earlier the spies told Israel they were like grasshoppers in the Canaanites' eyes. All along, it was the Canaanites who were afraid.

insights.title: Unlikely faith
insights.body: The first person in Canaan to confess Yahweh is a prostitute in an enemy city. Whom might you have written off who is closer to faith than you think?

3.summary: Israel crosses the Jordan in flood behind the ark carried by the priests, as the river's waters stop and stand in a heap upstream.
3.lookfor: Notice the distance kept from the ark, the moment the waters stop, and how the crossing echoes the Red Sea.

names.name: Adam
names.gloss: A town on the Jordan about 30 kilometres upstream, where the waters piled up.

names.name: Zarethan
names.gloss: A town near Adam in the Jordan valley.

names.name: Salt Sea
names.gloss: The Dead Sea, where the Jordan ends.

insights.title: Keep your distance
insights.body: The people must stay "about two thousand cubits" behind the ark, about a kilometre (3:4), "that you may know the way by which you must go; for you have not passed this way before." The distance shows reverence and lets the whole nation see where to go.

insights.title: A second Red Sea
insights.body: The waters stop and Israel crosses "on dry ground" (3:17), as their parents did at the Red Sea. The new generation now has its own crossing. Joshua makes the parallel explicit in the next chapter, and Elijah and Elisha later divide the Jordan in the same area.

insights.title: In flood season
insights.body: "The Jordan overflows all its banks all the time of harvest" (3:15), the spring barley harvest when snowmelt from Mount Hermon swells the river. Israel crosses at the worst possible time, so the miracle is unmistakable.

insights.title: Blocked at Adam
insights.body: The waters "rose up in one heap, a great way off, at Adam" (3:16), usually identified with Tell ed-Damiyeh. Historical records describe the Jordan being blocked near there by collapsing banks in 1267 and after an earthquake in 1927. Some see God using such an event; the text stresses the timing, as the priests' feet touched the water.

insights.title: The Lord of all the earth
insights.body: The ark is "the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth" (3:11). The title claims that Yahweh rules not just Israel but the land of Canaan and every nation. The living God goes before them (3:10).

insights.title: Feet first
insights.body: The waters stop only "when the soles of the feet of the priests... rest in the waters" (3:13). The priests have to step into a flooded river before anything happens. Obedience comes before the miracle.

insights.title: You have not passed this way
insights.body: "You have not passed this way before" (3:4). What new path are you facing where you need to keep your eyes on what God is doing ahead of you?

4.summary: Twelve men carry stones from the riverbed to build a memorial at Gilgal, Joshua sets up twelve more in the Jordan, and the river returns once the priests come out.
4.lookfor: Notice the two sets of stones, the question children will ask, and the date Israel enters the land.

names.name: Gilgal
names.gloss: Israel's first camp west of the Jordan, near Jericho, and a base for years.

insights.title: What do these stones mean?
insights.body: The stones are for the day "when your children ask in the future, saying, 'What do you mean by these stones?'" (4:6). Like the Passover meal, the memorial is designed to provoke a question so that parents can tell the story.

insights.title: Two memorials
insights.body: Twelve stones are carried to Gilgal (4:20), and Joshua sets up twelve more in the middle of the Jordan where the priests stood, "and they are there to this day" (4:9). One memorial could be visited; the other would be hidden under the river once it returned.

insights.title: The tenth day of the first month
insights.body: Israel comes up out of the Jordan "on the tenth day of the first month" (4:19). That is the day on which, in Exodus, families chose their Passover lambs. Four days later they keep the Passover in the land (5:10).

insights.title: The eastern tribes cross
insights.body: About forty thousand armed men of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh cross ahead of the others (4:12-13), "as Moses spoke to them." Their wives and children remain east of the river. The promise of Numbers 32 is being kept.

insights.title: So that all peoples may know
insights.body: The crossing happened "that all the peoples of the earth may know that Yahweh's hand is mighty" (4:24). God's acts for Israel are meant to be seen by the nations. Rahab had already shown how news of the Red Sea spread.

insights.title: Joshua magnified
insights.body: "On that day, Yahweh magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel; and they feared him, as they feared Moses" (4:14). The crossing confirms God's promise in 3:7. A new leader is established not by his own claims but by God's acts.

insights.title: Your memorial stones
insights.body: Israel marked what God had done with stones their children would ask about. What reminders of God's faithfulness have you set up for those who come after you?

5.summary: At Gilgal the new generation is circumcised and keeps the Passover, the manna stops, and Joshua meets the commander of Yahweh's army near Jericho.
5.lookfor: Notice why the circumcision was needed, what ends when they eat the produce of the land, and the stranger's answer to Joshua's question.

names.name: Gilgal
names.gloss: The camp near Jericho, named for God "rolling away" Israel's reproach.

insights.title: Circumcised before the battle
insights.body: The men born in the wilderness had not been circumcised (5:5), so Joshua circumcises them right in enemy territory (5:2-8). Militarily it was a risky moment. Covenant identity came before conquest.

insights.title: Gilgal: rolled away
insights.body: "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you" (5:9). The Hebrew galal, "to roll," sounds like Gilgal, the place's name. The shame of slavery, and perhaps of the wilderness failure, is removed.

insights.title: Passover in the land
insights.body: Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month (5:10), the first in the land and only the third recorded. Only the circumcised could eat it, which explains why the circumcision came first.

insights.title: The manna stopped
insights.body: "The manna ceased on the next day, after they had eaten of the produce of the land" (5:12). For forty years God fed them directly; now he feeds them through the land's harvest. The miracle ends exactly when it is no longer needed.

insights.title: Neither side
insights.body: Joshua asks the armed man, "Are you for us, or for our enemies?" He answers, "No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh's army" (5:13-14). The question is not whether God is on Israel's side, but whether Israel is on God's.

insights.title: Take off your shoes
insights.body: "Take off your shoes; for the place on which you stand is holy" (5:15). Moses heard almost the same words at the burning bush. Joshua's call is shown to match his master's.

insights.title: Whose side?
insights.body: Joshua wanted to know whose side the commander was on. How often do you ask God to be on your side, rather than asking whether you are on his?

6.summary: Israel marches around Jericho once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh; at the trumpet blast and shout the wall falls, the city is destroyed, and Rahab's family is spared.
6.lookfor: Notice the role of the ark and the priests, the number seven, the silence until the shout, and what happens to Rahab.

names.name: Rahab
names.gloss: The woman of Jericho who hid the spies and is spared with her family.

insights.title: Sevens everywhere
insights.body: Seven priests carry seven ram's-horn trumpets, the army circles for seven days, and seven times on the seventh day (6:4). The battle is shaped like a week of worship ending in a sabbath. The ark at the centre shows whose victory it is.

insights.title: Shofar
insights.body: The "trumpets of rams' horns" (6:4) are the shofar, the horn still blown in synagogues at Rosh Hashanah and at the end of Yom Kippur. Here it announces God's judgment on Jericho.

insights.title: Silent marching
insights.body: For six days the people must not shout or say a word (6:10). Only the trumpets sound. The long silence makes the final shout all the more dramatic.

insights.title: Jericho and the archaeologists
insights.body: Jericho is one of the oldest cities in the world. Excavators have argued for decades over its walls: John Garstang dated a destruction to around 1400 BC, Kathleen Kenyon concluded the city was largely unoccupied in Joshua's time, and others have challenged her dating. The question is still debated.

insights.title: Devoted to Yahweh
insights.body: The city is "devoted" (6:17): every person and animal is killed (6:21), and its metals go to Yahweh's treasury (6:19). This is cherem, total dedication to God through destruction. It is one of the hardest scenes in Scripture, and readers have long wrestled with it; the text presents it as judgment and as Israel's first fruits of the land given wholly to God.

insights.title: Rahab saved
insights.body: "Rahab the prostitute, her father's household, and all that she had, Joshua saved alive" (6:25). The spies kept their oath. Hebrews says the walls fell "by faith," and in the same breath praises Rahab's faith.

insights.title: The curse on Jericho
insights.body: Joshua curses anyone who rebuilds Jericho: it will cost him his firstborn and youngest sons (6:26). In Ahab's reign, Hiel of Bethel rebuilt it at exactly that cost, "according to Yahweh's word."

insights.title: Victory by worship
insights.body: Jericho fell to marching, trumpets and a shout rather than siege weapons. Where are you tempted to rely on your own strategies when God may be asking for trust?

7.summary: Israel is defeated at Ai because Achan secretly took devoted plunder from Jericho; after lots expose him, he confesses and is stoned with his family in the valley of Achor.
7.lookfor: Notice how Israel's confidence leads to defeat, Joshua's prayer, how the guilty man is found, and what he says about what he saw.

names.name: Achan
names.gloss: A man of Judah who took forbidden plunder from Jericho.

names.name: Ai
names.gloss: A town east of Bethel whose name means "the ruin."

names.name: Beth Aven
names.gloss: A place near Bethel; the name means "house of wickedness."

names.name: Bethel
names.gloss: A town in the central hill country where Jacob dreamed of the ladder.

names.name: valley of Achor
names.gloss: "The valley of trouble," where Achan was executed.

insights.title: One man, whole nation
insights.body: The chapter opens, "the children of Israel committed a trespass" (7:1), though only Achan took the plunder. God says, "Israel has sinned" (7:11). The covenant people are treated as one body, so one man's hidden sin affects all.

insights.title: Overconfidence at Ai
insights.body: The scouts say only two or three thousand men are needed for such a small town (7:3). Nobody asks God. Thirty-six men die and "the hearts of the people melted, and became like water" (7:5), the very words used of the Canaanites.

insights.title: Get up!
insights.body: Joshua tears his clothes and complains that God brought them across only to destroy them (7:7). God answers, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face like that?" (7:10). There is a time for prayer and a time to deal with the sin.

insights.title: Found by lot
insights.body: Israel is brought near tribe by tribe, clan by clan, household by household, man by man (7:14-18), probably by casting sacred lots. The narrowing search gives Achan every chance to come forward first. Saul later uses the same method to find Jonathan.

insights.title: I saw, I coveted, I took
insights.body: Achan confesses: "When I saw... then I coveted them and took them" (7:21), the same pattern as Eve in Eden. Among his loot was "a beautiful Babylonian robe," literally a robe from Shinar.

insights.title: Kept back part
insights.body: The Greek translation describes Achan's sin with the verb for embezzling, the same rare word Luke uses when Ananias and Sapphira kept back part of the price of their land. Both stories come at the start of a new chapter for God's people.

insights.title: His family too
insights.body: Achan is stoned along with his sons, daughters and animals (7:24-25). This is deeply troubling, especially since Deuteronomy forbids putting children to death for their parents' sins. Some interpreters think the family must have shared in hiding the loot in the tent; the text does not say.

insights.title: A door of hope
insights.body: The place is named the valley of Achor, "trouble" (7:26). Hosea later promises that God will give "the valley of Achor for a door of hope." The place of judgment becomes a picture of new beginnings.

8.summary: With God's direction Joshua takes Ai by ambush, then builds an altar on Mount Ebal, writes the law on stones and reads the blessings and curses to all Israel.
8.lookfor: Notice how the earlier defeat is turned into a strategy, Joshua's outstretched javelin, and who hears the law read at the end.

names.name: Ai
names.gloss: The town that defeated Israel in chapter 7.

names.name: Mount Ebal
names.gloss: A mountain beside Shechem where Moses had commanded an altar to be built.

names.name: Mount Gerizim
names.gloss: The mountain facing Ebal, where half the tribes stood.

insights.title: Don't be afraid
insights.body: God's first words after the Achan affair are, "Don't be afraid, and don't be dismayed" (8:1). This time Israel may take the plunder and livestock (8:2), which was forbidden at Jericho. Achan's theft was needless.

insights.title: Using the defeat
insights.body: Joshua plans to flee "like the first time" (8:6) so that Ai's men chase them out of the city while an ambush takes it. The earlier humiliation becomes the bait.

insights.title: The outstretched javelin
insights.body: Joshua stretches out his javelin toward Ai and does not draw back his hand until the city is destroyed (8:18, 8:26). It recalls Moses holding up his hands during the battle with Amalek, with Joshua then leading the fighting.

insights.title: Where was Ai?
insights.body: Ai is usually identified with et-Tell near Bethel, but excavations found it unoccupied for centuries before the period of Joshua. Some scholars treat the account as later tradition; others propose a different site nearby, such as Khirbet el-Maqatir. The location is still debated.

insights.title: Buried by sundown
insights.body: The king of Ai is hanged on a tree until evening and then taken down at sundown (8:29), following Deuteronomy's command that a body must not remain on a tree overnight. Joshua does the same with the five kings in chapter 10.

insights.title: Moses' command carried out
insights.body: Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal, writes a copy of Moses' law on stones, and reads the blessing and the curse with the tribes on both mountains (8:30-34). It is exactly what Moses had commanded. In the 1980s an archaeologist identified a stone structure on Ebal as this altar, a claim others dispute.

insights.title: Every word, to everyone
insights.body: "There was not a word of all that Moses commanded, which Joshua didn't read before all the assembly of Israel, with the women, the little ones, and the foreigners" (8:35). Right in the middle of the conquest, Israel stops to hear God's word together.

insights.title: After failure
insights.body: Ai, the place of Israel's defeat, becomes the place of victory and renewed worship. How has God brought something good from a failure in your life?

9.summary: The people of Gibeon trick Israel into a peace treaty by pretending to come from far away; when the truth comes out, Israel keeps its oath and makes them woodcutters and water carriers.
9.lookfor: Notice the props in the Gibeonites' disguise, what Israel failed to do, and why the leaders keep their oath anyway.

names.name: Gibeon
names.gloss: A large town about 10 kilometres northwest of Jerusalem.

names.name: Hivites
names.gloss: One of the peoples of Canaan, to which the Gibeonites belonged.

names.name: Kiriath Jearim
names.gloss: One of the Gibeonite towns, where the ark later stayed for twenty years.

insights.title: Mouldy bread and worn shoes
insights.body: The Gibeonites bring worn sacks, patched wineskins and shoes, old clothes and "dry and moldy" bread (9:4-5). They claim it was hot from the oven when they left (9:12). The props are designed to fit Deuteronomy's rule allowing peace with "cities which are very far off."

insights.title: They didn't ask
insights.body: "The men sampled their provisions, and didn't ask counsel from Yahweh's mouth" (9:14). Israel trusted what they could see and taste. The failure is not being tricked but making a decision without seeking God.

insights.title: An oath is an oath
insights.body: When the deception is discovered, the people murmur, but the leaders say, "We have sworn to them by Yahweh" (9:19). An oath in God's name binds even when obtained by trickery. The psalmist praises one who keeps an oath even when it hurts.

insights.title: Saul breaks the oath
insights.body: Centuries later, King Saul tried to wipe out the Gibeonites. God sent a famine in David's reign because of it, showing that Joshua's oath still stood.

insights.title: Woodcutters and water carriers
insights.body: The Gibeonites become "wood cutters and drawers of water" for the congregation and for God's altar (9:21, 9:27). Deuteronomy uses the same phrase for the humblest members of Israel's covenant assembly. Their punishment also brings them into service at God's house.

insights.title: Fear that leads to life
insights.body: The Gibeonites say they acted because they heard that God had commanded Israel to destroy the land's inhabitants, "Therefore we were very afraid for our lives" (9:24). Like Rahab, they believed what God had said. Men of Gibeon later helped rebuild Jerusalem's walls after the exile.

insights.title: Deciding without asking
insights.body: Israel looked at the evidence and decided without asking God. What decisions are you making based only on how things look?

10.summary: Five Amorite kings attack Gibeon; Israel marches all night to rescue it, God sends hailstones, the sun stands still at Joshua's prayer, and Joshua conquers the cities of the south.
10.lookfor: Notice why Israel fights for Gibeon, the two miracles in the battle, what happens to the five kings, and the repeated formula of conquest.

names.name: Adoni-Zedek
names.gloss: King of Jerusalem; his name means "lord of righteousness."

names.name: Lachish
names.gloss: A major fortified city in the Shephelah, southwest of Jerusalem.

names.name: Beth Horon
names.gloss: A pass running down from the hill country toward the coastal plain.

names.name: Aijalon
names.gloss: A valley west of Gibeon on the route to the coast.

names.name: Makkedah
names.gloss: A town in the lowlands where the five kings hid in a cave.

skim.advice: Verses 28 to 39 repeat the same formula as city after city is taken. Skim them, noticing the names, and read the battle at Gibeon and the summary in verses 40 to 42 closely.

insights.title: Lord of righteousness
insights.body: Jerusalem's king is Adoni-Zedek, meaning lord of righteousness (10:1), a name like Melchizedek, king of righteousness, the priest-king of Salem in Abraham's day. Letters found at Amarna in Egypt, from the 14th century BC, include several from a king of Jerusalem pleading for Egyptian help against raiders.

insights.title: Keeping a hard promise
insights.body: Gibeon's alliance with Israel makes it a target, and Israel marches all night from Gilgal to defend it (10:6-9). The treaty obtained by deception in chapter 9 is honoured at real cost, and God gives victory through it.

insights.title: Hailstones
insights.body: "There were more who died from the hailstones than those whom the children of Israel killed with the sword" (10:11). The narrator makes sure the credit goes to God. Isaiah remembers what God did "in the valley of Gibeon."

insights.title: Sun, stand still
insights.body: Joshua's prayer, "Sun, stand still on Gibeon! You, moon, stop in the valley of Aijalon!" (10:12), is quoted from "the book of Jashar" (10:13), a lost collection of poems. Interpreters understand it as a literal miracle, as poetic language for a victory won in a single day, or as a request for the sun to stop shining, such as darkness or an eclipse. All agree the text stresses that Yahweh listened.

insights.title: No day like it
insights.body: "There was no day like that before it or after it, that Yahweh listened to the voice of a man; for Yahweh fought for Israel" (10:14). The wonder is not only the sun but that God heeded a human request so dramatically.

insights.title: Feet on their necks
insights.body: Joshua's captains put their feet on the necks of the five kings (10:24), an ancient gesture of total victory shown in Egyptian and Assyrian art. Psalm 110 promises the Messiah that God will make his enemies a footstool for his feet.

insights.title: Formula and reality
insights.body: The repeated phrase "he left no one remaining" (10:28-39) describes the southern campaign in sweeping terms. Yet later chapters show cities like Hebron and Debir still needing to be taken (15:13-15). Many scholars see this as the stock language of ancient war reports, which often described victories as total.

insights.title: Yahweh fought for Israel
insights.body: Twice the chapter says Yahweh fought for Israel (10:14, 10:42). What battles in your life do you need to hand over to God?

11.summary: Jabin king of Hazor leads a northern coalition against Israel; Joshua defeats them at the waters of Merom, burns Hazor, and the summary declares the whole land taken after a long war.
11.lookfor: Notice the size of the enemy army, what Joshua does with the horses and chariots, why Hazor alone is burned, and the giants who remain.

names.name: Jabin
names.gloss: King of Hazor, leader of the northern Canaanite kings; the name may be a dynastic title.

names.name: Hazor
names.gloss: The largest city in Canaan, north of the Sea of Galilee.

names.name: waters of Merom
names.gloss: Springs in upper Galilee where the northern kings gathered.

names.name: Anakim
names.gloss: A clan of unusually tall people living in the hill country.

names.name: Gath
names.gloss: A Philistine city where some Anakim survived; Goliath's home town.

insights.title: As the sand on the seashore
insights.body: The northern army is "as the sand that is on the seashore in multitude, with very many horses and chariots" (11:4). Israel had no chariots. God's word to Joshua is the familiar one: "Don't be afraid" (11:6).

insights.title: Hamstrung horses
insights.body: God commands Joshua to hamstring the enemy horses and burn the chariots (11:6, 11:9). Israel was not to build its strength on chariots, as Deuteronomy warned kings. David later did much the same, keeping only a few.

insights.title: Hazor burned
insights.body: Hazor "used to be the head of all those kingdoms" (11:10), and it alone was burned (11:13). Excavations at Hazor, one of the largest sites in the region, uncovered a massive destruction by fire in the 13th century BC. Scholars debate who caused it, but the burning matches this account.

insights.title: Jabin again
insights.body: A later "Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor" oppresses Israel in the days of Deborah. Jabin may have been a royal title passed down, or Hazor may have revived.

insights.title: A long time
insights.body: "Joshua made war a long time with all those kings" (11:18). Caleb's ages in chapter 14 suggest about seven years of fighting. The swift, sweeping summaries cover years of hard campaigning.

insights.title: Hardened hearts
insights.body: "It was of Yahweh to harden their hearts, to come against Israel in battle" (11:20), so that no city except Gibeon sought peace (11:19). As with Pharaoh, the text holds God's purpose and the kings' choices together.

insights.title: Giants in Gath
insights.body: Joshua cut off the Anakim from the hill country, but "in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, did some remain" (11:22). Goliath of Gath, the giant David faced, came from one of these towns.

insights.title: The land had rest
insights.body: The chapter ends, "The land had rest from war" (11:23). Hebrews says Joshua's rest was not the final one. What kind of rest are you longing for?

12.summary: A list of the kings Israel defeated: two east of the Jordan under Moses, and thirty-one west of the Jordan under Joshua.
12.lookfor: Notice the two halves, east under Moses and west under Joshua, and how many of the cities you have met in the story so far.

names.name: Sihon
names.gloss: Amorite king of Heshbon defeated under Moses.

names.name: Og
names.gloss: King of Bashan, defeated under Moses.

names.name: Megiddo
names.gloss: A strategic city guarding the pass into the valley of Jezreel.

names.name: Tirzah
names.gloss: A city later used as the capital of the northern kingdom.

skim.advice: Verses 9 to 24 are a list of thirty-one kings, each followed by "one." Skim the names, and read verses 1, 6 and 7 for the shape of the chapter.

insights.title: Moses and Joshua side by side
insights.body: The chapter lists the victories east of the Jordan under Moses (12:1-6) and west of the Jordan under Joshua (12:7-24) in matching form. Each gave the land to tribes "for a possession" (12:6, 12:7). Joshua completes what Moses began.

insights.title: One, one, one
insights.body: Each king is followed by "one" (12:9-24), as in a tally. The list probably reflects an ancient record or victory inscription. Egyptian kings carved similar lists of conquered towns on temple walls.

insights.title: Thirty-one kings
insights.body: Canaan was not one kingdom but many small city-states, each with its own king. That is why the total reaches thirty-one in a land smaller than many modern provinces. The Amarna letters show the same pattern of small rival kings in the 14th century BC.

insights.title: Names to come
insights.body: Many cities on this list return later in the Bible: Megiddo (12:21), where Solomon built and Josiah fell; Tirzah (12:24), a royal city of the northern kingdom; Jerusalem (12:10), not yet held by Israel. The list prepares the map for the books that follow.

insights.title: Kings defeated, land not yet taken
insights.body: Defeating a city's king was not the same as occupying its land. The very next chapter begins, "there remains yet very much land to be possessed" (13:1). The list celebrates victories while the story goes on.

insights.title: Remembering victories
insights.body: Israel kept a list of what God had done. What would you put on a list of the battles God has won for you?

13.summary: God tells the aged Joshua that much land remains to be taken and that he must divide it anyway; the chapter then records the land Moses gave east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh.
13.lookfor: Notice the list of land not yet taken, the repeated note about Levi, and the peoples Israel did not drive out.

names.name: Philistines
names.gloss: Sea Peoples settled on the southern coast in five cities, later Israel's great rivals.

names.name: Geshurites
names.gloss: A small kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee that Israel never removed.

names.name: Gebalites
names.gloss: People of Gebal, the Phoenician port later called Byblos.

names.name: Medeba
names.gloss: A town on the plateau east of the Dead Sea.

names.name: Balaam
names.gloss: The seer hired by Moab to curse Israel, killed among the Midianites.

names.name: Mahanaim
names.gloss: A town in Gilead where Jacob saw angels; later David's refuge.

skim.advice: Most of the chapter traces the borders and towns of the eastern tribes. Read the opening verses 1 to 7 and the notes in verses 13, 14, 22 and 33, and skim the town lists.

insights.title: Old, with much land left
insights.body: God says plainly, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to be possessed" (13:1). The book that said Joshua "took the whole land" (11:23) now admits the work is unfinished. Both statements stand side by side.

insights.title: Divide it anyway
insights.body: Even with the Philistine coast and Lebanon still unconquered, God tells Joshua, "Just allocate it to Israel for an inheritance" (13:6). The tribes receive land by promise before they hold it in fact. Their task is to take what is already assigned.

insights.title: The five lords of the Philistines
insights.body: The Philistines had "five lords" (13:3) ruling Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron. They were part of the Sea Peoples who settled the coast around the 12th century BC, and remain Israel's chief enemy through Samson, Saul and David.

insights.title: Geshur survives
insights.body: "The children of Israel didn't drive out the Geshurites, nor the Maacathites" (13:13). David later married Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur, and their son Absalom fled to Geshur after killing his brother.

insights.title: Levi's inheritance
insights.body: Twice the chapter says Levi received no land: their inheritance is the offerings made by fire (13:14) and "Yahweh, the God of Israel, is their inheritance" (13:33). The tribe without territory is a reminder that the land itself belongs to God.

insights.title: Balaam's end
insights.body: In the middle of a boundary list comes a note that Israel killed "Balaam the son of Beor, the soothsayer" (13:22). The seer who could not curse Israel is remembered here simply as a diviner.

insights.title: Unfinished work
insights.body: Joshua was old and the job was not done. How do you think about work God gives you that you may not see completed?

14.summary: The division of the land west of the Jordan begins by lot, and Caleb, now eighty-five, claims Hebron as Moses had promised for his faithfulness as a spy.
14.lookfor: Notice how the land is divided, Caleb's account of his own life, and his attitude to the giants still in Hebron.

names.name: Eleazar
names.gloss: The high priest, Aaron's son, who oversees the dividing of the land.

names.name: Caleb
names.gloss: One of the twelve spies, who with Joshua urged Israel to trust God.

names.name: Kenizzite
names.gloss: A clan originally listed among the peoples of Canaan, whose members joined Judah.

names.name: Kiriath Arba
names.gloss: The old name of Hebron, "city of Arba," named after a great man of the Anakim.

insights.title: By lot
insights.body: The land is distributed "by the lot of their inheritance" (14:2) under Eleazar the priest and Joshua. Casting lots before God was trusted to reveal his choice rather than human favouritism. Moses had ordered it so.

insights.title: Caleb the Kenizzite
insights.body: Caleb is "the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite" (14:6). The Kenizzites appear in Genesis among the peoples of Canaan, so Caleb's family may have been outsiders who joined Judah. If so, one of Israel's most faithful heroes came from outside its bloodline.

insights.title: Eighty-five and still strong
insights.body: Caleb was forty when he spied the land and is now eighty-five (14:7, 14:10). "As my strength was then, even so is my strength now" (14:11). The forty-five years give a timeline: thirty-eight years of wandering and about seven of conquest.

insights.title: Wholly followed
insights.body: Caleb says three times that he "wholly followed Yahweh" (14:8, 14:9, 14:14). The phrase echoes God's verdict on him in Numbers and Deuteronomy. His reward was promised at Kadesh and is received forty-five years later.

insights.title: Give me this hill country
insights.body: Caleb asks for the hardest assignment: the hill country where "the Anakim were there, and great and fortified cities" (14:12). The giants that frightened the other spies forty-five years earlier are exactly what Caleb wants to face, trusting that "Yahweh will be with me."

insights.title: Hebron
insights.body: Hebron, once called Kiriath Arba (14:15), was where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Jacob were buried. Caleb receives the place where the promise to the patriarchs was first anchored in the land. David was later crowned king there.

insights.title: Giants at eighty-five
insights.body: Caleb asked for a hard task in old age. What would it look like for you to keep trusting God for big things at every stage of life?

15.summary: Judah's borders and towns are listed in detail, with the story of Caleb taking Hebron and Debir and his daughter Achsah asking for springs, and a note that the Jebusites of Jerusalem could not be driven out.
15.lookfor: Trace Judah's four borders, notice the short story of Achsah, and read the final verse about Jerusalem.

names.name: valley of Hinnom
names.gloss: The valley just south of Jerusalem, later notorious for child sacrifice.

names.name: Achsah
names.gloss: Caleb's daughter, who asks her father for springs of water.

names.name: Othniel
names.gloss: Caleb's kinsman who captures Debir; later Israel's first judge.

names.name: Kiriath Sepher
names.gloss: The old name of Debir; it means "city of the book" or "of the scribe."

names.name: En Gedi
names.gloss: An oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea where David later hid from Saul.

names.name: Jebusites
names.gloss: The people who held Jerusalem until David captured it.

skim.advice: Verses 1 to 12 trace Judah's borders and verses 20 to 62 list its towns by region. Skim them, and read Caleb and Achsah's story (verses 13 to 19) and the final verse closely.

insights.title: Judah first
insights.body: Judah receives the first and largest allotment west of the Jordan, and its description is the longest. It fits Judah's leading role from Jacob's blessing onward, the tribe of David and of the kings in Jerusalem.

insights.title: The valley of Hinnom
insights.body: Judah's border runs "by the valley of the son of Hinnom" (15:8), just south of Jerusalem. Later kings sacrificed children there, and Josiah defiled the site. Its Hebrew name, Ge Hinnom, became Gehenna, the word Jesus uses for the place of final judgment.

insights.title: The city of the book
insights.body: Debir used to be called Kiriath Sepher (15:15), probably "city of the book" or "of the scribe." The name suggests it was a place of records or writing in Canaanite times.

insights.title: Achsah asks for springs
insights.body: Caleb gives his daughter to Othniel as a prize, but Achsah takes the initiative: "Give me a blessing... give me also springs of water" (15:19). Her land in the dry south needed water. The same scene appears in Judges, where Othniel becomes the first judge.

insights.title: Driving out the giants
insights.body: "Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak: Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai" (15:14). They are the same three names the spies saw at Hebron forty-five years earlier. The man who believed then is the one who finishes the job.

insights.title: Jerusalem not taken
insights.body: "As for the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah couldn't drive them out" (15:63). The future holy city stays in Canaanite hands until David captures it. Judges says the same of Benjamin.

insights.title: Ask for springs
insights.body: Achsah saw what her land lacked and asked her father for it. What are you lacking that you could ask your Father for?

16.summary: The territory of the Joseph tribes is described, focusing on Ephraim's borders, with a note that the Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out but put to forced labour.
16.lookfor: Notice the shared allotment of Joseph's sons and the closing note about Gezer.

names.name: Bethel
names.gloss: A town on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin, important in Jacob's story.

names.name: Luz
names.gloss: The old name of Bethel, or a site close to it.

names.name: Gezer
names.gloss: A Canaanite city guarding the route from the coast into the hills.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The tribe descended from Joseph's younger son, which became the leading northern tribe.

skim.advice: This short chapter traces borders by place names. Skim them, and read the opening and the note about Gezer in verse 10.

insights.title: Joseph's double share
insights.body: "The children of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, took their inheritance" (16:4). Jacob had adopted Joseph's two sons as his own, so Joseph receives two tribal portions, the double share of a firstborn.

insights.title: Ephraim before Manasseh
insights.body: Ephraim's border is described first, though Manasseh was the elder. Jacob had crossed his hands to bless the younger above the older, and Ephraim became so prominent that the northern kingdom was later called by its name.

insights.title: Gezer remains
insights.body: "They didn't drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer... and have become servants to do forced labor" (16:10). Instead of removing them, Ephraim made them labourers. Gezer stayed Canaanite until an Egyptian pharaoh captured it and gave it to Solomon as a dowry.

insights.title: Gezer's walls and stones
insights.body: Gezer was a major city on the route from the coast to Jerusalem. Excavations there uncovered a massive gate from the time of Solomon, a row of standing stones from much earlier, and the Gezer Calendar, one of the oldest known Hebrew inscriptions, listing the farming months.

insights.title: Cities within Manasseh
insights.body: Some of Ephraim's cities lay "in the middle of the inheritance of the children of Manasseh" (16:9). The two Joseph tribes' lands were intertwined, as the next chapter shows with Tappuah.

insights.title: Settling for less
insights.body: Ephraim chose cheap labour over finishing what God commanded. Where might you be settling for a convenient compromise?

17.summary: Manasseh's land is described, Zelophehad's daughters receive their promised inheritance, and when the Joseph tribes complain their land is too small, Joshua tells them to clear the forested hills.
17.lookfor: Notice the women who receive land, the Canaanite cities Manasseh could not take, and Joshua's answer to the complaint.

names.name: Machir
names.gloss: Manasseh's eldest son, whose clan took Gilead and Bashan.

names.name: Zelophehad
names.gloss: A man of Manasseh who died leaving five daughters and no sons.

names.name: Beth Shean
names.gloss: A strong city where the Jezreel valley meets the Jordan valley.

names.name: Megiddo
names.gloss: A fortified city guarding the main pass into the Jezreel valley.

names.name: valley of Jezreel
names.gloss: The broad fertile plain across northern Israel, ideal for chariots.

insights.title: The daughters receive their land
insights.body: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah come before Eleazar and Joshua and say, "Yahweh commanded Moses to give us an inheritance" (17:4). They receive it. The case they brought in Numbers is completed here.

insights.title: Ten parts
insights.body: "Ten parts fell to Manasseh... because the daughters of Manasseh had an inheritance among his sons" (17:5-6). The daughters' shares are counted alongside the male clans. Their petition changed the map.

insights.title: Couldn't drive them out
insights.body: "The children of Manasseh couldn't drive out the inhabitants of those cities" (17:12), including Beth Shean, Taanach and Megiddo. When Israel grew strong they made the Canaanites forced labourers instead (17:13). Judges records the same failure.

insights.title: Chariots of iron
insights.body: The Canaanites of the valleys "have chariots of iron" (17:16), probably wooden chariots with iron fittings. Chariots ruled the flat plains like Jezreel but were of little use in the hills, which is why Israel settled first in the highlands.

insights.title: Clear the forest
insights.body: When the Joseph tribes complain of too little land, Joshua says, "go up to the forest, and clear land for yourself" (17:15). The central hill country was then wooded. Archaeology shows hundreds of small new villages appearing in these hills in the early Iron Age.

insights.title: Joshua's reply
insights.body: The Joseph tribes say, "we are a numerous people" (17:14). Joshua, himself an Ephraimite, turns their boast back on them: if you are so many and so strong, then clear the forest and drive out the Canaanites (17:17-18). He gives them work, not favouritism.

insights.title: Big enough to work
insights.body: Joshua answered a complaint about too little with a call to hard work. Where might God be calling you to develop what you have rather than ask for more?

18.summary: Israel sets up the tabernacle at Shiloh, and Joshua sends surveyors to map the remaining land so that it can be divided by lot among the last seven tribes, beginning with Benjamin.
18.lookfor: Notice Joshua's question to the seven tribes, how the land is surveyed, and Benjamin's position between Judah and Joseph.

names.name: Shiloh
names.gloss: A town in Ephraim's hill country where the tabernacle stood for generations.

names.name: Benjamin
names.gloss: The small tribe descended from Jacob's youngest son, settled between Judah and Ephraim.

names.name: stone of Bohan
names.gloss: A landmark on the border of Judah and Benjamin, named after a Reubenite.

skim.advice: Verses 11 to 28 trace Benjamin's borders and towns. Read verses 1 to 10 closely and skim the lists.

insights.title: The tent at Shiloh
insights.body: "The whole congregation... assembled themselves together at Shiloh, and set up the Tent of Meeting there" (18:1). Shiloh became Israel's religious centre until Samuel's time. Jeremiah later points to its ruin as a warning to Jerusalem.

insights.title: How long will you neglect?
insights.body: Joshua asks seven tribes, "How long will you neglect to go in to possess the land?" (18:3). Some tribes had grown comfortable. The land was given, but they had to go and take it.

insights.title: Surveying the land
insights.body: Three men from each tribe walk through the land and describe it "by cities into seven portions in a book" (18:9). Ancient rulers had land surveyed for taxes and boundaries; here the survey serves a fair division by lot.

insights.title: Lots before Yahweh
insights.body: Joshua casts the lots "here before Yahweh in Shiloh" (18:8, 18:10). Doing it at the sanctuary makes the division an act of worship and puts it beyond quarrelling.

insights.title: Benjamin in the middle
insights.body: Benjamin's land falls "between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph" (18:11), the two most powerful tribes. Its towns include Jericho, Gibeon, Ramah and "the Jebusite (also called Jerusalem)" (18:28). Israel's first king, Saul, came from this small tribe.

insights.title: Jerusalem on the border
insights.body: The border between Judah and Benjamin runs through the valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem (18:16). Jerusalem sat on the boundary of the two tribes, which later made it a fitting capital for David to unite north and south.

insights.title: Neglecting what is given
insights.body: "How long will you neglect to go in to possess the land?" What has God given you that you have not yet stepped into?

19.summary: The remaining six lots go to Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and Dan, and finally Israel gives Joshua his own town, Timnathserah.
19.lookfor: Notice where Simeon's land lies, Dan's move north, and who receives land last.

names.name: Beersheba
names.gloss: A town in the far south, linked with Abraham and Isaac.

names.name: Gath Hepher
names.gloss: A town in Zebulun, the home of the prophet Jonah.

names.name: Shunem
names.gloss: A town in Issachar where Elisha later raised a boy to life.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: The great Phoenician port city on the coast north of Israel.

names.name: Chinnereth
names.gloss: A town on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, which was named after it.

names.name: Leshem
names.gloss: A northern town captured by Dan and renamed Dan.

names.name: Timnathserah
names.gloss: Joshua's own town in the hill country of Ephraim.

skim.advice: Most of the chapter lists borders and towns for six tribes. Skim the names, and read the notes in verses 1, 9, 47 and 49 to 51.

insights.title: Simeon inside Judah
insights.body: Simeon's inheritance was "in the middle of the inheritance of the children of Judah" (19:1), because Judah's share was too large (19:9). Jacob had said Simeon and Levi would be scattered in Israel. Simeon gradually merged into Judah, and Moses' blessing does not mention it.

insights.title: A second Bethlehem
insights.body: Zebulun's towns include a Bethlehem (19:15) in Galilee, different from the Bethlehem of Judah where David and Jesus were born. Micah and Matthew name Bethlehem with Ephrathah or Judea, which keeps the two apart.

insights.title: Towns with later stories
insights.body: Gath Hepher in Zebulun (19:13) was the home of the prophet Jonah. Shunem in Issachar (19:18) was where Elisha raised a woman's son. Many names in these lists come alive later in the Bible.

insights.title: Asher and the sea
insights.body: Asher's border reaches "to great Sidon" and "the fortified city of Tyre" (19:28-29), the great Phoenician ports. Israel never held them, and Judges notes that Asher lived among the Canaanites on the coast.

insights.title: Dan moves north
insights.body: Dan's border "went out beyond them" when the tribe captured Leshem in the far north and renamed it Dan (19:47). Squeezed by the Amorites and Philistines in its original land, Dan migrated. Judges tells the full and troubling story.

insights.title: The leader goes last
insights.body: Only after every tribe has its land does Israel give Joshua his town, Timnathserah, which he asked for (19:49-50). The leader receives his inheritance last, and he has to build the city himself.

insights.title: Last of all
insights.body: Joshua waited until everyone else had received their share. Where could you put others' needs before your own?

20.summary: Israel designates six cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan, where someone who kills by accident can flee from the avenger of blood until trial.
20.lookfor: Notice what the person fleeing must do at the city gate, how long they stay, and who else may use these cities.

names.name: Kedesh
names.gloss: A city of refuge in the hills of Naphtali in Galilee.

names.name: Shechem
names.gloss: A city of refuge between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.

names.name: Bezer
names.gloss: A city of refuge east of the Jordan in Reuben's territory.

names.name: Ramoth
names.gloss: Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge in Gad's territory.

names.name: Golan
names.gloss: A city of refuge in Bashan, in Manasseh's territory east of the Jordan.

insights.title: Promised long before
insights.body: God reminds Joshua of the cities "of which I spoke to you by Moses" (20:2). Exodus, Numbers and Deuteronomy all speak of them. Now they are finally named and set apart.

insights.title: At the gate
insights.body: The person fleeing must "stand at the entrance of the gate of the city, and declare his case in the ears of the elders" (20:4). This detail is new: the elders give him a place to live while he awaits trial. Refuge begins with telling the truth.

insights.title: Spread across the land
insights.body: Kedesh in the north, Shechem in the centre and Hebron in the south lie west of the Jordan; Bezer, Ramoth and Golan lie east (20:7-8). Each part of the country had a refuge within reach. All six were also Levite towns.

insights.title: Unintentionally
insights.body: The cities are for anyone who kills "accidentally or unintentionally" (20:3), literally in error and without knowledge. The same idea of unintended sin appears in Leviticus' sin offerings. Intention matters before God.

insights.title: For the alien too
insights.body: The cities serve "all the children of Israel, and for the alien who lives among them" (20:9). Protection from vengeance was not limited to citizens.

insights.title: Until the high priest dies
insights.body: The killer stays "until the death of the high priest that shall be in those days" (20:6). Christian readers have long seen a picture of Christ, the high priest whose death sets people free, and Hebrews speaks of believers who have fled for refuge to the hope set before them.

insights.title: Running for refuge
insights.body: These cities were for people who had done real harm. Where do you run when guilt, deserved or not, is chasing you?

21.summary: The Levites receive forty-eight towns with pastures from the other tribes, and the chapter ends by declaring that God gave Israel all the land and rest, and that not one of his good promises failed.
21.lookfor: Notice how the Levite clans are spread across all the tribes, which towns go to Aaron's descendants, and the great summary at the end.

names.name: Kohathites
names.gloss: The Levite clan to which Aaron's priestly family belonged.

names.name: Gershon
names.gloss: Levi's son, whose clan receives towns in the north.

names.name: Merari
names.gloss: Levi's son, whose clan receives towns in Zebulun and east of the Jordan.

names.name: Anathoth
names.gloss: A priestly town in Benjamin, later the home of Jeremiah.

skim.advice: Verses 9 to 40 list the towns given to each Levite clan. Skim them, and read the opening request and the summary in verses 41 to 45 closely.

insights.title: Asking for what was promised
insights.body: The Levite leaders come to Eleazar and Joshua at Shiloh and say, "Yahweh commanded through Moses to give us cities" (21:2). Like Caleb and Zelophehad's daughters, they claim a promise already made.

insights.title: Scattered by design
insights.body: The Levites receive forty-eight towns spread through every tribe (21:41). Jacob had said Levi would be scattered in Israel as a punishment; it becomes a blessing, putting teachers of God's law within reach of every Israelite.

insights.title: Priests near Jerusalem
insights.body: Aaron's descendants receive thirteen towns in Judah, Simeon and Benjamin (21:4, 21:19), all fairly close to the future site of the Temple. Anathoth, one of them (21:18), was later the hometown of the priest-prophet Jeremiah.

insights.title: Hebron shared
insights.body: Hebron itself goes to the priests, but "the fields of the city and its villages" go to Caleb (21:12). Both the faithful spy's reward and the priests' needs are honoured.

insights.title: Not one word failed
insights.body: "Nothing failed of any good thing which Yahweh had spoken to the house of Israel. All came to pass" (21:45). Joshua repeats it in his farewell, and Solomon says it again when he dedicates the Temple.

insights.title: All the land, yet not yet
insights.body: "Yahweh gave to Israel all the land" and "rest all around" (21:43-44), yet chapters 13 to 19 listed many places not taken. The summary speaks from God's side: every promise was kept and the land was theirs to hold. Whether Israel would fully take hold of it was their responsibility.

insights.title: All came to pass
insights.body: Looking back, Israel could say not one of God's promises failed. Which of God's promises have you seen come true?

22.summary: Joshua sends the eastern tribes home with blessing; they build a large altar by the Jordan, the other tribes prepare for war, but the eastern tribes explain it is a witness, not a rival altar, and peace is kept.
22.lookfor: Notice why the western tribes are alarmed, the past sins they recall, and how the misunderstanding is resolved.

names.name: Phinehas
names.gloss: Son of the high priest Eleazar, known for his zeal at Peor.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: The hilly region east of the Jordan settled by Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh.

names.name: Achan
names.gloss: The man whose theft at Jericho brought defeat on all Israel.

insights.title: Promise kept
insights.body: Joshua tells the eastern tribes, "You have not left your brothers these many days" (22:3). They kept their pledge from Numbers 32 through years of war. They go home "with much wealth" and share the plunder with their brothers (22:8).

insights.title: Why the alarm?
insights.body: Deuteronomy allowed sacrifice only at the one place God would choose. A second great altar looked like rebellion, and the western tribes remembered Peor and Achan, when one group's sin brought judgment on all (22:17, 22:20).

insights.title: Talk before fighting
insights.body: Israel gathers for war, but first sends Phinehas and ten leaders to ask (22:12-14). They even offer to share their own land if the eastern land is "unclean" (22:19). Investigating before acting saved a civil war.

insights.title: The Mighty One, God, Yahweh
insights.body: The eastern tribes answer with a solemn oath: "The Mighty One, God, Yahweh, the Mighty One, God, Yahweh, he knows" (22:22). In Hebrew it is El, Elohim, Yahweh, three names for God repeated twice. The same triple title opens Psalm 50.

insights.title: An altar for remembering
insights.body: The altar was not for sacrifice but "a witness between us and you" (22:27), so that future generations would not say the eastern tribes had "no portion in Yahweh" (22:25). They feared the river would become a religious border. They named it "A Witness Between Us that Yahweh is God" (22:34).

insights.title: Unity across a river
insights.body: The Jordan could easily have divided Israel. Later history shows the eastern tribes were indeed vulnerable and among the first taken into exile. This chapter shows a moment when misunderstanding was settled by honest words rather than swords.

insights.title: Assume or ask?
insights.body: The western tribes nearly went to war over a misunderstanding. When something looks wrong, do you ask before you assume?

23.summary: In old age Joshua gathers Israel's leaders and urges them to stay faithful to God, warning that if they mix with the remaining nations and serve their gods, those nations will become snares and they will lose the land.
23.lookfor: Notice what Joshua says God has done, the warning about the nations that remain, and his words about his own death.

insights.title: Two farewells
insights.body: Joshua gives two farewell speeches, this one to the leaders and the next to all the tribes at Shechem. Like Moses' farewell in Deuteronomy, both look back on God's faithfulness and forward to the danger of turning away.

insights.title: God fought for you
insights.body: "It is Yahweh your God who has fought for you" (23:3), Joshua says, and again in 23:10. The old general takes no credit for the victories.

insights.title: One chases a thousand
insights.body: "One man of you shall chase a thousand; for it is Yahweh your God who fights for you" (23:10). The Song of Moses used the same picture in reverse: one chasing a thousand of Israel when God had abandoned them.

insights.title: Hold fast
insights.body: "Hold fast to Yahweh your God" (23:8) uses davaq, the verb for clinging, as a husband to his wife. The opposite danger is to "hold fast to the remnant of these nations" through intermarriage (23:12). Israel must cling to one or the other.

insights.title: Thorns in your eyes
insights.body: The remaining nations will become "a snare and a trap to you, a scourge in your sides, and thorns in your eyes" (23:13). Moses had warned the same, and Judges records God saying they would be thorns in Israel's sides.

insights.title: The way of all the earth
insights.body: "Today I am going the way of all the earth" (23:14) was a gentle way of saying that death was near. King David uses the same words to Solomon on his deathbed.

insights.title: Good things and evil things
insights.body: "Not one thing has failed of all the good things" God promised (23:14), so Israel can be just as sure he will bring "all the evil things" if they break the covenant (23:15). God's faithfulness cuts both ways.

insights.title: Clinging
insights.body: Joshua calls Israel to cling to God as they had so far. What are you holding on to most tightly right now?

24.summary: At Shechem Joshua retells God's story from Abraham to the conquest, challenges Israel to choose whom they will serve, makes a covenant with them, and dies; Joseph's bones are buried and Eleazar dies.
24.lookfor: Notice who does all the acting in the history, Joshua's challenge and the people's answers, the stone witness, and the three burials at the end.

names.name: Shechem
names.gloss: A city between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim where Abraham built an altar and Jacob bought land.

names.name: Terah
names.gloss: Abraham's father, who worshipped other gods in Mesopotamia.

names.name: Nahor
names.gloss: Abraham's brother, who stayed in Mesopotamia.

names.name: Timnathserah
names.gloss: Joshua's town in the hill country of Ephraim, where he was buried.

names.name: Hamor
names.gloss: The ruler of Shechem from whose sons Jacob bought a field.

names.name: Phinehas
names.gloss: Eleazar's son, in whose hill Eleazar was buried.

insights.title: I took, I gave, I sent
insights.body: Joshua's history speaks in God's voice: "I took your father Abraham... I sent Moses... I brought you... I gave you a land" (24:3-13). It begins with Abraham's family serving other gods beyond the Euphrates (24:2). Grace comes before the call to obey.

insights.title: Not with your sword
insights.body: God drove out the Amorites "not with your sword, nor with your bow" (24:12), and gave them a land they had not worked for, cities they did not build, vineyards they did not plant (24:13). A psalm says the same: they did not win the land by their own arm.

insights.title: As for me and my house
insights.body: "Choose today whom you will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh" (24:15). The choice is not between God and nothing, but between Yahweh and other gods. Elijah later sets the same choice before Israel on Mount Carmel.

insights.title: You can't serve Yahweh
insights.body: When the people promise to serve God, Joshua answers, "You can't serve Yahweh, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God" (24:19). He presses them so that their commitment is not easy or shallow. Three times they insist, and he makes them witnesses against themselves (24:22).

insights.title: Under the oak at Shechem
insights.body: Joshua tells them to "put away the foreign gods which are among you" (24:23) and sets up a great stone "under the oak" by the sanctuary (24:26). At the same place Jacob once buried his household's foreign gods under the oak by Shechem.

insights.title: A stone that heard
insights.body: "This stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all Yahweh's words" (24:27). Ancient covenants were often recorded on standing stones. The stone stays as a silent reminder of what Israel promised.

insights.title: A hundred and ten
insights.body: Joshua dies at 110 (24:29), the same age as Joseph. The book then buries Joseph's bones at Shechem (24:32), fulfilling the oath Israel made to him in Egypt. Hebrews counts his request about his bones as an act of faith.

insights.title: While the elders lived
insights.body: "Israel served Yahweh all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua" (24:31). The faithfulness lasted one generation. Judges opens with the next generation, "who didn't know Yahweh."

intro.who: The Talmud credits Joshua with writing the book, apart from the account of his death. Many modern scholars see it as part of a larger history running from Deuteronomy to Kings, built from older traditions and shaped during the monarchy and the exile.
intro.when: It follows straight on from Moses' death, traditionally dated around 1400 BC or, on a later reckoning, the 13th century BC. Archaeologists debate how much of the conquest the evidence supports, and many see Israel's emergence in the hill country as gradual.
intro.why: It shows God keeping his promise of the land as Israel crosses the Jordan, wins key battles, divides the land by lot and renews the covenant, while also admitting that much land remained unconquered and calling each generation to choose whom it will serve.
